subtopic_detail: first line management of a persistent head tilt with a palpable neck mass in early infancy
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 7 week old girl brought by her parents because her head is always tilted. She was delivered by forceps after a prolonged second stage.

Her parents noticed a firm pea sized lump in the right side of her neck at about three weeks of age, which has not changed since. Her head tilts to the right and her chin points to the left, and they find it hard to turn her face to the right when settling her. She is feeding well, gaining weight along the 50th centile, and moves all four limbs equally. Her eye movements are full in all directions.

data_table.Examination: Head tilted to the right with chin rotated to the left, firm non tender 1 cm mass within the right sternocleidomastoid, passive rotation of the head to the right limited to about 50 degrees, tone and reflexes normal in all four limbs
data_table.Investigations: No investigations performed, red reflex present and symmetrical, hips clinically stable on Ortolani and Barlow testing

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for surgical release of the sternocleidomastoid within a month
options.rationale: Surgical release is considered only after a sustained conservative programme has failed, conventionally not before twelve months of age. Operating at seven weeks removes the chance of the spontaneous resolution that most infants achieve. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

options.text: Arrange urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical spine
options.rationale: Imaging is reserved for atypical features such as a tilt that is not accompanied by rotation to the opposite side, abnormal tone or reflexes, developmental regression, or failure to respond to an adequate physiotherapy programme. Her examination is otherwise normal and imaging at this age would require sedation. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

options.text: Refer to physiotherapy for a stretching and positioning programme
options.rationale: Passive stretching, positioning to encourage active rotation toward the restricted side and parent education resolve the great majority of cases when started in the first few months. Earlier referral produces better and faster correction, which is why this is done now rather than after a period of observation. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

options.text: Arrange botulinum toxin injection of the shortened neck muscle
options.rationale: Botulinum toxin has been used as an adjunct in resistant cases in older children, but it is not a first line intervention and the evidence in infancy is limited. It would be considered only well after a stretching programme had failed. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

options.text: Reassure the parents that no intervention is needed at this age
options.rationale: Untreated restriction leads to progressive facial asymmetry and positional flattening of the skull, and the window in which stretching works best is the first few months. Reassurance alone forfeits that window. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

explanation.summary: Congenital muscular torticollis presents in the first weeks to months of life with the head tilted toward the affected sternocleidomastoid and the chin rotated away from it, and a firm painless mass within the muscle is present in a proportion of cases and resolves over several months. Difficult instrumental delivery and intrauterine crowding are the usual antecedents. The two associations to check at the same visit are developmental dysplasia of the hip, which shares the crowding aetiology and occurs more often in these infants, and positional plagiocephaly, which develops because the infant persistently rests on the same part of the skull. Physiotherapy with passive stretching and active positioning resolves most cases, with better outcomes the earlier it starts. Features that should redirect the assessment include a tilt without contralateral chin rotation, abnormal tone, limitation that is painful, an eye movement abnormality suggesting ocular torticollis, or failure to improve over several months of an adequate programme.
key_points: The head tilts toward the affected muscle and the chin rotates away from it
Start physiotherapy early rather than observing, because outcomes are time dependent
Check the hips at the same visit given the shared association with crowding
Watch for positional plagiocephaly and facial asymmetry developing
Reserve surgery for failure of conservative treatment after about twelve months
explanation.pearls: A head tilt without the expected chin rotation to the opposite side is not muscular torticollis and should prompt assessment for an ocular cause, a posterior fossa lesion or an atlantoaxial abnormality rather than a physiotherapy referral.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

subtopic_detail: timing of repair for a reducible groin swelling in a young ex preterm infant
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in the outpatient clinic seeing a 6 week old boy born at 32 weeks gestation. His parents noticed a bulge in his right groin about ten days ago, which appears when he cries or strains and settles when he is asleep.

It is present when you examine him. He is feeding well, has had no vomiting, opens his bowels normally and his nappies are unremarkable. The swelling extends downwards from the groin toward the scrotum, and you are unable to feel a normal cord above it. It flattens with steady gentle pressure and the right testis is palpable separately below the swelling. The left side is normal.

data_table.Examination: Right groin swelling extending toward the scrotum, upper border not palpable, reducible with gentle sustained pressure, overlying skin normal in colour with no tenderness, right testis palpable separately in the scrotum, abdomen soft and not distended
data_table.Investigations: Weight tracking along the 25th centile, no investigations performed, no vomiting and no abdominal distension reported

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure the parents that this resolves on its own by twelve months
options.rationale: Spontaneous closure over the first year is the natural history of a communicating hydrocele, which is why this option is tempting in an infant with a scrotal swelling. A hernia containing bowel does not close spontaneously, and the inability to feel normal cord above the swelling separates the two at the bedside. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal Hernia)

options.text: Arrange a groin ultrasound and review in the clinic in three months
options.rationale: The diagnosis is clinical and ultrasound adds little when the examination findings are as clear as these. A three month delay in an infant of this age spans the period of greatest incarceration risk. (Source: Royal Australasian College of Surgeons)

options.text: Arrange emergency theatre tonight for exploration of the right groin
options.rationale: Emergency operation is required for an irreducible swelling, particularly with tenderness, discolouration, vomiting or abdominal distension, none of which he has. His swelling reduces with gentle pressure and he is feeding and passing stool normally. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal Hernia)

options.text: Refer to paediatric surgery for repair on the next available list
options.rationale: A reducible groin hernia in early infancy carries a high risk of incarceration, greatest in the first months of life and higher again in babies born preterm, so repair is arranged promptly rather than deferred. Referral while it remains reducible allows an elective operation instead of an emergency one. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal Hernia)

options.text: Advise observation with review only if the swelling becomes painful
options.rationale: Waiting for pain means waiting for incarceration, which presents with an irreducible tender lump and can progress to bowel and testicular ischaemia within hours. Emergency repair in that setting carries substantially higher complication rates than elective repair. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal Hernia)

explanation.summary: Inguinal hernia in infancy is almost always indirect and results from a patent processus vaginalis, the same embryological structure whose incomplete obliteration produces a communicating hydrocele. The clinical distinction rests on whether the upper border of the swelling can be felt: a hydrocele confined to the scrotum allows the examiner to palpate normal cord above it and typically transilluminates, whereas a hernia extends up through the inguinal canal so that no upper border is reachable. Prematurity is the strongest risk factor and incidence rises steeply with decreasing gestational age. The clinical urgency comes from incarceration, which is far more common in infancy than in later childhood and threatens both the bowel and the ipsilateral testis through compression of the gonadal vessels. Because of this, hernias in young infants are repaired promptly on an elective list, whereas hydroceles are observed and usually resolve by around two years without intervention.
key_points: A patent processus vaginalis underlies both infant hernia and communicating hydrocele
Inability to palpate normal cord above the swelling indicates a hernia
Prematurity markedly increases both incidence and incarceration risk
Incarceration threatens bowel and the ipsilateral testis within hours
Hydroceles are observed to about two years, hernias are repaired promptly
explanation.pearls: The risk of incarceration in an untreated infant inguinal hernia is highest in the first six months of life and is reported at around 30 per cent in infants under one year, which is why repair is arranged within weeks rather than deferred until the child is older and larger.

subtopic_detail: proceeding to division of a restrictive lingual frenulum after optimised attachment has failed
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 9 day old breastfed boy in the assessment unit. His mother describes severe pain throughout every feed and her nipples are cracked and bleeding.

He feeds for about fifty minutes and wants to feed again within ninety minutes. A lactation consultant has seen the pair twice over the past four days and has worked on positioning and attachment at both visits, with no improvement in pain or in the pattern of feeding. His birth weight was 3480 g. On examination his tongue cannot be lifted above the level of the lower gum and the tip is notched when he cries.

data_table.Examination: Frenulum attached close to the tip of the tongue restricting elevation and lateral movement, tongue tip notched on crying, palate intact, no ankyloglossia of the upper lip, mother's nipples cracked with a compressed shape after the feed
data_table.Investigations: Weight 3090 g, representing 11 per cent below birth weight, serum bilirubin below the treatment threshold for age, no fever

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Advise cessation of breastfeeding and establish full formula feeding
options.rationale: Abandoning breastfeeding forecloses a problem with an effective and simple treatment. It should be a decision the mother reaches after the remediable cause has been addressed, not a first line clinical recommendation. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association)

options.text: Supply nipple shields for the mother and review the weight in one week
options.rationale: Shields can reduce pain in the short term but often reduce milk transfer further, which is the opposite of what a baby who has lost 11 per cent of his birth weight needs. Waiting a further week without addressing transfer risks continued weight loss. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association)

options.text: Commence formula top up feeds after each breastfeed and review weekly
options.rationale: Supplementation may well be needed in the short term to protect his weight and would reasonably run alongside the definitive step, but used alone it leaves the mechanical restriction and the maternal pain untreated and predictably ends breastfeeding. (Source: RCH CPG: Breastfeeding)

options.text: Treat both mother and baby for candida and review in one week
options.rationale: Candidal infection causes burning nipple pain that characteristically persists between feeds and is often accompanied by oral plaques in the infant, whereas her pain is confined to the feed and the nipple emerges compressed, which indicates a mechanical problem. There are no oral plaques. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Refer for division of the tongue tie after the review of attachment
options.rationale: A frenulum that restricts tongue elevation, combined with nipple trauma, prolonged ineffective feeding and weight loss that has not responded to two skilled attachment reviews, is the specific situation in which frenotomy improves maternal pain and feeding effectiveness. Division is a brief procedure that allows immediate feeding afterwards. (Source: RCH CPG: Breastfeeding)

explanation.summary: Ankyloglossia describes a lingual frenulum short or anteriorly attached enough to restrict tongue movement, and it is present in a meaningful minority of newborns, though only a fraction of those have any feeding problem at all. This distinction governs practice: the anatomical finding alone is not an indication to operate, and rates of division rose substantially in Australia before that point was re-emphasised. The indication combines a restrictive frenulum on examination with a genuine functional problem, meaning nipple pain and trauma, ineffective milk transfer with poor weight gain, or prolonged unsatisfying feeds, that has not resolved with skilled assessment of positioning and attachment. Weight loss beyond about 10 per cent of birth weight is itself a marker requiring prompt action regardless of cause. Frenotomy is performed without general anaesthesia in young infants, bleeding is usually minimal and the infant can feed immediately, with maternal pain scores improving most consistently in trials.
key_points: The anatomical finding alone is never the indication for division
Combine a restrictive frenulum with a documented functional feeding problem
Skilled attachment review must come first and be seen to fail
Weight loss beyond about 10 per cent of birth weight requires prompt action
Maternal nipple pain is the outcome that improves most consistently after frenotomy
explanation.pearls: A nipple that emerges compressed into a wedge or lipstick shape at the end of a feed indicates a mechanical compression problem rather than infection, and it distinguishes a restrictive tongue tie from candidal nipple pain, which burns between feeds as well as during them.
